title: How do you design a reliable benchmark for a JVM service? Explain the warmup phase and JIT compilation from C1 to C2, accounting for GC cycles, using HdrHistogram, isolating the bottleneck, and initialising the connection pool before measuring.
shortTitle: How to design a JVM benchmark?

s1_definition.profdef: A reliable JVM benchmark separates a warmup phase from a measurement phase, because the HotSpot JVM starts by interpreting bytecode, then the C1 (client) compiler produces lightly optimised native code, and finally the C2 (server) compiler produces heavily optimised code once a method is hot. You must also let garbage-collection cycles reach steady state, pre-initialise expensive resources like connection pools and caches, record latency into a lossless structure such as HdrHistogram rather than averaging, and isolate the component under test so you measure it and not the network, the database, or the load generator.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine timing how fast a new teller at National Bank of India serves customers. On the first morning the teller is slow — reading the manual for every step (interpreting bytecode). After a few dozen customers they remember the common steps (C1 compilation). After a few hundred they are an expert moving on autopilot (C2 compilation). If you time them in the first ten minutes, you record the beginner, not the expert who will actually run the branch for the next year. A good benchmark lets the teller become expert first (warmup), makes sure the cash drawer is already stocked (connection pool initialised), ignores the one coffee break (does not confuse a GC pause with normal work by measuring long enough), and writes down every single service time (HdrHistogram) instead of just the average.
s1_definition.oneliner: A trustworthy JVM benchmark warms up until C2 has compiled the hot path and GC is steady, pre-initialises pools and caches, records every latency into HdrHistogram, and isolates the one component under test.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A reliable JVM benchmark separates a warmup phase from a measurement phase, because the HotSpot JVM starts by interpreting bytecode, then the C1 (client) compiler produces lightly optimised native code, and finally the C2 (server) compiler produces heavily optimised code once a method is hot. You must also let garbage-collection cycles reach steady state, pre-initialise expensive resources like connection pools and caches, record latency into a lossless structure such as HdrHistogram rather than averaging, and isolate the component under test so you measure it and not the network, the database, or the load generator.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine timing how fast a new teller at National Bank of India serves customers. On the first morning the teller is slow — reading the manual for every step (interpreting bytecode). After a few dozen customers they remember the common steps (C1 compilation). After a few hundred they are an expert moving on autopilot (C2 compilation). If you time them in the first ten minutes, you record the beginner, not the expert who will actually run the branch for the next year. A good benchmark lets the teller become expert first (warmup), makes sure the cash drawer is already stocked (connection pool initialised), ignores the one coffee break (does not confuse a GC pause with normal work by measuring long enough), and writes down every single service time (HdrHistogram) instead of just the average.

**One line to remember:** A trustworthy JVM benchmark warms up until C2 has compiled the hot path and GC is steady, pre-initialises pools and caches, records every latency into HdrHistogram, and isolates the one component under test.

sections.s2_technical:
HotSpot runs tiered compilation. A method starts interpreted, which is slow. As a method's invocation and loop-back-edge counters cross thresholds, the JVM compiles it with C1, giving fast-ish code plus profiling counters. When those counters show the method is truly hot, C2 recompiles it with aggressive optimisations like inlining, escape analysis and loop unrolling. This is why early iterations are much slower than steady state. If you measure before C2 kicks in, you benchmark the interpreter and C1, not the production hot path. The warmup phase exists to drive the hot methods all the way to C2 before you start recording. You can observe this with `-XX:+PrintCompilation`, which logs each compilation, and the number after the method is the tier.

Warmup must exercise the real code path with realistic data so the JIT profiles the branches your production traffic takes. For example, if ninety percent of transfers are domestic and ten percent international, warm up with that mix, otherwise C2 may optimise for the wrong branch and then deoptimise under real traffic. A subtle trap is dead-code elimination: if the benchmark does not use its result, C2 may delete the work entirely and you measure nothing. The fix is to consume the result, for example by accumulating it into a field or returning it to a blackhole. The Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH) handles warmup, forking a fresh JVM, and blackholes for you; you annotate with `@Warmup(iterations = 5)`, `@Measurement(iterations = 10)`, `@BenchmarkMode(Mode.SampleTime)`, and consume results via a `Blackhole` parameter.

Garbage collection must reach steady state. Early in a run the heap is small and young-generation collections are infrequent; as caches fill and the live set grows, collection frequency and pause behaviour change. If you measure for only a few seconds you may catch zero full collections and report a fantasy. You should run long enough to see several GC cycles, log them with `-Xlog:gc*`, and either include their effect in your latency (because real users feel pauses) or deliberately exclude a known one-off like class-loading. Fixing the heap with equal initial and maximum sizes, for example `-Xms4g -Xmx4g`, removes heap-resizing noise during the run.

Latency must be recorded losslessly. Averages hide everything; a mean of five milliseconds can hide a p99 of five hundred. HdrHistogram records every value into logarithmically sized buckets so you get accurate high percentiles at low memory cost. You create one with `new Histogram(maxValue, significantDigits)`, record with `histogram.recordValue(latencyUs)`, and read percentiles with `histogram.getValueAtPercentile(99.9)`. In long runs you also want interval histograms so an early slow period does not dominate the whole run — HdrHistogram's `Recorder` gives you non-blocking interval snapshots via `recorder.getIntervalHistogram()`.

Isolating the bottleneck means ensuring you measure the component you intend to. Pre-initialise everything expensive before the measurement window: open the connection pool and run a warmup query so HikariCP has created its minimum-idle connections, prime caches, and establish TLS sessions, because a cold pool creating connections lazily will add tens of milliseconds to the first requests and pollute the histogram. Run the load generator on a separate host so its CPU does not steal from the service. Pin the test to avoid noisy neighbours, disable CPU frequency scaling where possible, and change one variable at a time. If you want to measure pure CPU logic, stub the database; if you want to measure the database path, make sure the pool is warm and the dataset is representative. The senior-level nuance is that a benchmark answers exactly one question, so you decide the question first — "what is the p99 of fee calculation on a warm JVM" is a different experiment from "what is the p99 of the full endpoint including the database" — and you design the isolation accordingly.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India needs to benchmark its interest-calculation service, which computes daily interest on savings accounts. The first naive benchmark timed one thousand iterations in a cold JVM and reported eighty microseconds, but production showed twelve microseconds after a while. The team was measuring the interpreter, not the optimised hot path.

Problem 1 — the JVM was cold, so the first iterations ran interpreted and under C1, dragging the average up. This is exactly why a warmup phase is needed: we run tens of thousands of untimed iterations first so C2 compiles the calculation method before we record anything.

Problem 2 — the naive benchmark threw away the result, so C2 could have deleted the calculation as dead code. This is exactly the dead-code-elimination trap: we must consume every result, which we do by accumulating into a sink field.

Problem 3 — the real service reads account data through a connection pool, and the cold pool added latency to the first calls. This is exactly the connection-pool-initialisation requirement: we pre-open the pool and run a priming query before the measurement window so we measure calculation plus a warm read, not pool creation.

Problem 4 — the naive benchmark reported only an average, hiding the tail. This is exactly why we record into HdrHistogram and report median, p99 and p99.9 instead of a single mean.

The code will have an `InterestCalculator` with the hot calculation method, a `WarmPoolProvider` that simulates pre-initialising a connection pool, and a `BenchmarkRunner` that performs an explicit warmup phase, then a measurement phase recording into HdrHistogram, consuming every result into a sink, and printing proper percentiles. A `BenchmarkDemo` main class ties it together and logs the warmup-versus-measured difference.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package

# Run with GC + compilation logging so you can SEE warmup reach C2 and GC steady
java -Xms2g -Xmx2g \
     -XX:+PrintCompilation \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,level,tags \
     -cp target/classes:$(cat cp.txt) com.bank.bench.BenchmarkDemo

# The real, production-grade version uses JMH:
#   @Warmup(iterations=5, time=1) @Measurement(iterations=10, time=1)
#   @Fork(2) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.SampleTime) with a Blackhole param
mvn -Pjmh clean verify
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a request to benchmark `dailyInterest` for account SAV2001 with a balance of one million rupees at six and a half percent annual rate. We run fifty thousand warmup iterations and two hundred thousand measured iterations.

Step 1 — the runner first calls `initialiseAndPrime` on the pool, which simulates the thirty-millisecond cost of opening connections and running a priming query. This cost happens before any timing, so it never enters the histogram. The bottleneck we care about is isolated from pool startup.

Step 2 — the warmup loop runs fifty thousand untimed iterations. Early iterations run interpreted, then C1 compiles `dailyInterest`, and by the time the counters are hot C2 recompiles it with inlining and escape analysis. Each result is stored into the volatile sink so C2 cannot delete the work as dead code. No latency is recorded during this phase.

Step 3 — the measurement loop runs two hundred thousand iterations. For each, it reads a warm balance, records the start nanotime, runs the now-C2-optimised calculation, computes the latency in nanoseconds, and records it into the HdrHistogram. The result still flows into the sink.

Step 4 — because the loop runs long enough, several young-generation GC cycles occur as short-lived BigDecimal objects are allocated and collected. Those pauses show up as a small number of high-latency samples in the histogram, which is honest because real callers would feel them too.

Step 5 — the demo reads percentiles from the histogram: the median reflects the fast C2 steady state, around a handful of microseconds, while p99 and p99.9 capture the occasional GC pause. The reported numbers describe the optimised hot path, not the cold interpreter.

Step 6 — the final result value and the percentiles are logged, with a warning that only the measurement-phase numbers should be reported. The difference between this and the naive cold measurement is the whole point: the naive eighty microseconds was interpreter noise; the warm median is the real cost.

```
Oct 20, 2026 11:56:02 PM com.bank.bench.BenchmarkDemo main
INFO: Connection pool initialised and primed (SELECT 1 run)
INFO: WARMUP: 50000 untimed iterations (drive C1->C2)...
INFO: MEASURE: 200000 timed iterations into HdrHistogram...
INFO: RESULT dailyInterest=178.08 | median=0.420us p99=0.900us p99.9=11.300us max=240.000us
WARNING: Report percentiles from the MEASURE phase only — never the cold warmup.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Benchmark request: dailyInterest(SAV2001, 1,000,000, 6.5%)
    │
    ▼
  initialiseAndPrime()  ── 30ms pool open + SELECT 1 ──┐
    │  (OUTSIDE timing window — bottleneck isolated)    │ excluded
    ▼                                                   ▼
  WARMUP phase (50,000 iters, UNTIMED)           [no histogram records]
    │ interpret → C1 compile → C2 compile (hot)
    │ sink = result  (defeats dead-code elimination)
    ▼
  MEASURE phase (200,000 iters, TIMED)
    │ read warm balance
    │ t0 = nanoTime
    │ result = calc.dailyInterest(...)   ◄── C2-optimised hot path
    │ latency = nanoTime - t0
    │ histogram.recordValue(latency)
    │ (several young-GC pauses appear as tail samples)
    ▼
  HdrHistogram → median 0.42us / p99 0.9us / p99.9 11.3us
    │
    ▼
  Report MEASURE percentiles only  (never the cold warmup)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A reliable JVM benchmark has to respect how the JVM actually runs code. HotSpot starts by interpreting bytecode, then the C1 compiler produces lightly optimised native code with profiling, and finally the C2 compiler produces heavily optimised code once a method is proven hot. That means the first iterations are far slower than steady state, so I always run an explicit warmup phase that drives the hot methods all the way to C2 before I record a single number. If I measure a cold JVM I am benchmarking the interpreter, not the production hot path, which is exactly the mistake that made our interest service look like eighty microseconds when it was really a few.

I also guard against the traps that silently corrupt results. The biggest is dead-code elimination: if the benchmark throws away its result, C2 can delete the work entirely, so I consume every result into a sink field or a blackhole. I pre-initialise anything expensive outside the measurement window — I open the connection pool and run a priming query so HikariCP has created its minimum-idle connections and the TLS sessions are established — because a cold pool creating connections lazily would add tens of milliseconds to the first requests and pollute the histogram. That is how I isolate the bottleneck: I decide the one question the benchmark answers and I make sure nothing else leaks into the timing.

Garbage collection has to reach steady state too. Early in a run the heap is small and collections are rare; as the live set grows the pause behaviour changes, so I run long enough to see several cycles, I fix the heap with equal initial and maximum sizes to remove resizing noise, and I log collections so I can tell a GC pause apart from real work. I let those pauses show up in the latency because real callers feel them.

Finally, I never report averages. A mean hides the tail completely, so I record every latency into an HdrHistogram, which keeps accurate high percentiles cheaply, and I report median, p99 and p99.9 from the measurement phase only. For the production-grade version I use JMH, which handles warmup, forking a fresh JVM, and blackholes for me through annotations. At National Bank of India this discipline turned our benchmarks from misleading cold-JVM numbers into stable, trustworthy percentiles that we gate every release against, failing the build if the median or p99 regresses beyond a threshold.
